title: The Middle Ages · Episode 2
chapters: Byzantium: the Roman Empire that didn't fall

units.t: The Middle Ages. Episode two.
In this episode: 1066: the year England changed hands, Byzantium: the Roman Empire that didn't fall, The Islamic Golden Age and The Crusades.
Part one. 1066: the year England changed hands.
In a single autumn, England's king fought two invasions, marched hundreds of kilometres and died on a ridge in Sussex.
The country that came out the other side would never be the same.
Three claimants, one crown.
Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without children and with no obvious heir.
The English council quickly chose Harold Godwinson, the richest and most powerful earl in the kingdom, and he was crowned the very next day.
Two other men believed the crown was theirs.
William, Duke of Normandy, a distant relative of Edward, claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support him.
Across the North Sea, Harald Hardrada, King of Norway and one of the most famous warriors of his age, claimed it through an older agreement between earlier kings.
Both began preparing invasions, and Harold had to guard a long coastline without knowing who would strike first.
Two invasions in one month.
Harold spent the summer waiting for William on the south coast, but the Normans were held in port by unfavourable winds.
In September, with supplies low, Harold sent much of his army home.
Almost immediately, Harald Hardrada landed in the north with a large fleet, joined by Harold’s exiled brother, Tostig.
They defeated the northern earls at Fulford on 20 September.
Harold marched north astonishingly fast and surprised the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge on 25 September.
It was a crushing victory: Hardrada and Tostig were both killed, and the age of great Viking invasions of England is often said to end there.
Three days later, on 28 September, William’s army landed at Pevensey in Sussex.
The battle on the ridge.
Harold raced south again and took up a strong position on a ridge about ten kilometres from Hastings, where the town of Battle stands today.
His soldiers formed a shield wall, a dense line of overlapping shields bristling with spears and long-handled Dane axes.
William’s army combined archers, heavy infantry and mounted knights.
All day on 14 October the Normans attacked uphill, and all day the wall held.
A rumour spread that William was dead, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show his men his face.
Norman accounts describe retreats, some panicked and some possibly feigned, that lured English soldiers off the ridge to be cut down.
By evening Harold was dead, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, and the remaining army collapsed.
Not really a tapestry.
The Bayeux Tapestry is not technically a tapestry.
Tapestries are woven; this is embroidery, with coloured woollen threads stitched onto strips of linen.
It is around seventy metres long and half a metre tall, and tells the story like a comic strip.
It was likely commissioned by Bishop Odo, William’s half-brother, and many historians think English embroiderers made it.
It shows over six hundred people, horses, ships, Halley’s Comet and a few rude figures in the margins.
Its final section is lost.
The famous image of Harold’s death, a figure grasping an arrow near his eye, is debated.
It may be Harold, or the man beside him cut down by a knight, or both.
The tapestry was also restored in the nineteenth century, which may have altered the arrow.
What changed.
William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, but conquest took years.
Rebellions in the north were met with the Harrying of the North in 1069 and 1070, a campaign of deliberate destruction that caused famine across a huge region.
Within a generation, almost every great English landholder had been replaced by a Norman or other Frenchman.
Castles of earth and timber, then stone, appeared across the country, including the Tower of London.
At Christmas 1085, William ordered the Domesday Book, an extraordinary survey of who owned what across most of England.
French became the language of the court for centuries, which is why English has paired words: cow and beef, pig and pork, sheep and mutton.
The key idea: When Edward the Confessor died childless in 1066, three men claimed the English throne.
Part two. Byzantium: the Roman Empire that didn't fall.
When Rome fell in the West, its eastern half carried on for almost another thousand years.
From its glittering capital Constantinople, the Byzantine Empire kept Roman law, Greek learning and Christian art alive.
Rome's other half.
Most of us learn that the Roman Empire fell in AD 476, when the last emperor in the West was deposed.
But the eastern half carried on for nearly another thousand years.
Its people called themselves Romans, and its emperors saw themselves as heirs of Augustus.
'Byzantine' was popularised by European scholars long after the empire ended, taken from Byzantium, the old Greek town on whose site the capital was built.
Greek replaced Latin as its main language, but its rulers never stopped thinking of themselves as Roman.
In AD 330 Constantine dedicated Constantinople, now Istanbul, on the Bosporus, controlling the sea route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
Water guarded three sides, and Theodosius II's massive land walls guarded the fourth.
Justinian, Theodora and the law.
Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565, wanted to restore Rome's glory.
His generals reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, although holding them proved costly.
His wife Theodora, once an actress, a low-status job, became one of the most powerful women in Byzantine history.
During the Nika riots of 532, the historian Procopius records that she persuaded a wavering Justinian to stay and fight.
A terrible plague from 541 later killed a large share of the population.
After the riots, Justinian rebuilt Hagia Sophia, 537, in about five years.
For nearly a thousand years it was the world's largest cathedral.
It later became a mosque, a museum, and in 2020 a mosque again.
His Corpus Juris Civilis gathered Roman law into one collection and later shaped civil law systems.
Greek fire and gold coins.
In the late 600s, Arab fleets besieged Constantinople.
The Byzantines fought back with Greek fire, a burning liquid sprayed through tubes from ships that kept burning even on water.
Its recipe was a closely guarded state secret, so well guarded that we still do not know exactly what was in it.
Money mattered as much as weapons.
The gold solidus kept a stable gold content for several centuries, and merchants from Europe to Asia trusted it.
The empire also used diplomacy cleverly, paying neighbours, arranging marriages and setting enemies against each other.
Its survival owed as much to gold and cunning as to soldiers.
Faith, art and alphabets.
Religion was at the heart of Byzantine life.
Theological debates could spark riots, and arguments over religious images, known as iconoclasm, divided the empire in the 700s and 800s.
Differences grew between the Church in Constantinople and the Church in Rome, and in 1054 a formal split, the Great Schism, separated what became the Orthodox and Catholic churches.
In the 800s, two brothers from Thessaloniki, Cyril and Methodius, were sent as missionaries to the Slavs.
They created an alphabet for Slavic languages, and their followers developed the Cyrillic script, named for Cyril.
Today it is used for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and other languages, a living legacy of Byzantium across Eastern Europe.
The long fall.
The empire's greatest wound came from fellow Christians.
In 1204, knights of the Fourth Crusade, supposedly bound for the Holy Land, sacked Constantinople instead and looted its treasures.
The Byzantines recaptured their city in 1261, but the empire never recovered its strength.
Meanwhile the Ottoman Turks expanded steadily, until by the 1400s the empire was little more than the capital itself.
In 1453, Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople with a huge army and powerful cannons, and on 29 May the city fell.
The last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting.
Greek scholars who fled to Italy brought manuscripts with them, helping to fuel the Renaissance and carrying ancient Greek learning to the modern world.
The key idea: The eastern Roman Empire survived until 1453, and its well-placed, heavily walled capital helped it endure.
Part three. The Islamic Golden Age.
While much of Europe was fragmented, scholars in Baghdad, Cairo and Córdoba led the world in science, medicine and maths.
Empire and translation.
Islam began in Arabia in the early 600s.
Within a century, Arab armies built an empire from Spain to modern Pakistan, linking trade routes from the Atlantic to the borders of China.
The Abbasid dynasty founded Baghdad in 762, soon one of the world's largest cities.
The period from roughly the 700s to the 1200s is often called the Islamic Golden Age.
Caliphs like Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun sponsored translating Greek, Persian, Syriac and Sanskrit works into Arabic, with Baghdad's House of Wisdom a famous centre.
Muslims, Christians and Jews took part.
Paper, learned from China, made books cheaper.
Works by Aristotle, Galen and Ptolemy survived partly because they were translated and studied in Arabic.
Algebra and numerals.
Around 820, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations whose title included al-jabr, meaning restoring or completing: the origin of the word algebra.
Latin versions of his name gave us algorithm.
Arab mathematicians adopted the Indian number system, including zero and place value, and passed it on.
Europeans called them Arabic numerals, and the Italian Fibonacci promoted them in 1202.
Replacing clumsy Roman numerals, they made arithmetic, bookkeeping and science vastly easier.
Medicine and surgery.
Islamic cities built hospitals, called bimaristans, that treated patients regardless of wealth, kept records and trained doctors.
Al-Razi, Rhazes, distinguished smallpox from measles.
Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote The Canon of Medicine around 1025, a vast summary of medical knowledge that stayed a standard textbook in European universities into the 1600s.
In Córdoba, the surgeon al-Zahrawi described and illustrated hundreds of surgical instruments.
In the 1200s, Ibn al-Nafis correctly described blood circulating through the lungs, centuries before European scholars.
Light, stars and machines.
Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, wrote the Book of Optics in the early 1000s.
He showed that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays, as many Greeks had thought.
He studied lenses, mirrors and the camera obscura, and insisted on controlled experiments, so he's often cited as an early pioneer of the scientific method.
Astronomers built observatories, refined star tables and improved the astrolabe; star names like Aldebaran and Betelgeuse come from Arabic.
Engineers such as the Banu Musa brothers in the 800s and al-Jazari in 1206 wrote books of ingenious devices, including water clocks and automata that used cranks, valves and gears.
Cities, debate and legacy.
Learning flourished beyond Baghdad.

Córdoba was famed for its libraries and, by later tradition, lit and paved streets, and its philosopher Ibn Rushd, Averroes, defended reason so well that Europeans called him 'the Commentator' on Aristotle.
Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in 859, and Cairo's al-Azhar dates from 970.
In 1258 a Mongol army destroyed Baghdad, and later accounts say the Tigris ran dark with the ink of books thrown into it.
Learning continued elsewhere.
Through translations made in places like Toledo and Sicily, Arabic learning flowed into Europe, feeding universities and the Renaissance.
English still carries the trace in algebra, algorithm, alcohol, sugar and zero.
The key idea: Abbasid Baghdad became a centre of learning where Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic.
Part four. The Crusades.
For two centuries, European Christians launched military expeditions to the Holy Land.
The consequences are still debated today.
The call to crusade.
Jerusalem, holy to Christians, Jews and Muslims, had been under Muslim rule since the 600s.
In 1095, after the Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II preached at Clermont in France, urging Western Christians to fight.
He promised that those who went would have their sins forgiven.
Tens of thousands responded, from knights to ordinary people, motivated by faith, adventure, wealth and land.
They sewed cloth crosses onto their clothes; 'crusade' comes from the Latin crux, meaning cross.
The First Crusade.
Before the main armies even left, crusaders attacked Jewish communities in Rhineland cities like Mainz and Worms, massacring many people.
The main armies marched through Byzantine lands, besieged Antioch for months and, in 1099, captured Jerusalem, killing many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.
They set up four Crusader States along the eastern Mediterranean coast: Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli and the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
Their success owed much to divisions among local Muslim rulers.
Military orders soon formed to defend these states and protect pilgrims.
Saladin and Richard.
Muslim rulers gradually united.
Salah al-Din, known as Saladin, a Kurdish-born sultan of Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusader army at Hattin in 1187, trapping it far from water in summer heat.
He then retook Jerusalem, largely without the massacres of 1099, letting many inhabitants ransom themselves.
Even his enemies praised his honour and generosity.
The Third Crusade, 1189 to 1192, was led by Richard I of England, Philip II of France and Frederick Barbarossa, who drowned on the way.
Richard won battles, including Arsuf, but never retook Jerusalem.
He agreed a truce with Saladin allowing Christian pilgrims to visit, then was captured on his way home and held for a massive ransom.
Crusades gone astray.
In 1204, the Fourth Crusade, deep in debt to Venice for its ships, looted Constantinople, capital of the Christian Byzantine Empire.
The bronze horses now at St Mark's in Venice were among the spoils.
The betrayal deepened the split between Eastern and Western churches.
Crusades were also launched against pagans in the Baltic and Cathar heretics in France.
Frederick II regained Jerusalem in 1229 by treaty with barely any fighting, but it was lost again in 1244.
Louis IX of France was captured in Egypt in 1250 and ransomed, then died of disease near Tunis in 1270.
The Children's Crusade of 1212 is poorly recorded and partly legend.
The last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.
Orders and legacy.
The Knights Templar, founded around 1120, combined monastic vows with fighting.
They grew rich from donations and let pilgrims deposit money in Europe and draw it in the East.
In 1307, France's Philip IV, who owed them money, had them arrested on dubious charges, and the Pope dissolved the order in 1312.
The Crusades boosted Mediterranean trade, especially for Venice and Genoa, and brought European contact with Arabic goods and learning.
They also involved persecution of Jews and violence against Eastern Christians and Muslims.
Muslim writers of the time often saw crusaders as a frontier nuisance; the crusades loomed larger in later memory.
Understanding them means seeing several perspectives.
The key idea: In 1095, Pope Urban II urged Western Christians to fight for Jerusalem, promising forgiveness of sins.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why was the English throne contested in 1066?
Answer. Edward died childless, and three men claimed the crown.
Question two. What did the Byzantines consider themselves?
Answer. Romans, heirs of the Roman Empire.
Question three. How did scholars of the Islamic Golden Age help preserve Greek science?
Answer. By translating them into Arabic and studying them.
Question four. What did Pope Urban II promise those who went on crusade?
Answer. Forgiveness of their sins.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
